clinicalPearls: A rare congenital myopathy defined by peripheral, crescent-shaped caps of disorganised sarcomeres beneath the sarcolemma, rich in thin-filament proteins and lacking ATPase activity.
Associated most often with mutations in TPM2 and TPM3 (beta- and alpha-tropomyosin) and occasionally ACTA1.
Presents with congenital or childhood-onset hypotonia, proximal and facial weakness, an elongated myopathic face and a high-arched palate.
Respiratory involvement is common and is often the leading source of morbidity.
Regarded as part of the tropomyosin-related thin-filament myopathy spectrum, overlapping with nemaline myopathy and congenital fibre type disproportion.
Caps stain for actin, tropomyosin and alpha-actinin and are best demonstrated on oxidative and trichrome preparations.
Skeletal deformity, including scoliosis and chest-wall changes, may develop.
reference.pathophysiology: Cap myopathy arises from mutations, predominantly in tropomyosin genes, that alter regulation of the actin-myosin interaction and the calcium sensitivity of the thin filament. Mutant tropomyosin disturbs sarcomere assembly, producing peripheral subsarcolemmal zones of poorly organised, incompletely developed myofilaments (the caps) that are rich in thin-filament proteins. Impaired regulation of contraction underlies the muscle weakness.
additionalInvestigations: Muscle biopsy with oxidative, trichrome and immunohistochemical stains plus electron microscopy
Gene testing for TPM2, TPM3 and ACTA1
Pulmonary function and overnight respiratory studies
redFlags: Nocturnal hypoventilation or overt respiratory failure
Feeding and swallowing difficulty with aspiration risk
reference.prognosis: The disorder is usually static or slowly progressive, and long-term outlook depends chiefly on respiratory muscle involvement and orthopaedic complications, with many patients retaining ambulation.
pitfalls: Missing small caps when oxidative and immunostains are not performed.
Labelling the disease nemaline myopathy without recognising the cap pathology on the same thin-filament spectrum.
Not pursuing genetic confirmation for counselling.
references: Dubowitz V, Sewry CA, Oldfors A. Muscle Biopsy: A Practical Approach
International consensus guidance on the congenital myopathies
management: No disease-modifying drug therapy exists; management is supportive and directed at preserving respiratory and motor function
Respiratory surveillance with pulmonary function testing and overnight studies, introducing non-invasive ventilation for nocturnal hypoventilation
Physiotherapy and occupational therapy to maintain mobility and ambulation and to prevent contractures
Orthopaedic monitoring and management of scoliosis, including bracing or corrective spinal surgery
Anaesthetic precautions for this congenital myopathy, with heightened vigilance for perioperative respiratory compromise
Coordinated multidisciplinary neuromuscular care spanning respiratory, orthopaedic, physiotherapy and dietetic input
Genetic counselling and family screening given the underlying TPM2, TPM3 and ACTA1 mutations
